video_title: Why the Best Portfolios Are Built to Be Wrong | Systematic Investor | Ep. 411
gist: Convex Strategies CIO Dave Dredge and trend-following researcher Richard Brennan argue that markets are complex adaptive systems rather than Gaussian distributions, so risk is leverage and a shortage of loss-absorbing capital rather than volatility: calm markets are where fragility is manufactured (volatility targeting mechanically levers up while Value at Risk reports no risk), and Sharpe, Kelly and expected return all discard the path dependence that determines actual wealth. Evidence includes a Hong Kong-listed 2x SK Hynix ETF down 47% over three months while the stock is up 1%, an agent-based model in which a 25% population of trend-amplifying traders phase-shifts a Gaussian market into fat tails and volatility clustering, and a reshuffle of 40 years of returns that leaves Sharpe unchanged while terminal wealth falls 30-84%. Both conclude with the same prescription — engineer explicit convexity (long-dated mispriced optionality for Dredge, stops plus maximal diversification for Brennan), cap absolute leverage, and grow by widening the book rather than scaling bets.

themes.theme: July 2026 tape and Korean levered-ETF drag

insights.claim: As of late July 2026 trend-following indices were roughly flat for the month but held large year-to-date gains: BTOP50 -23bp in July and +8.32% YTD, SG CTA index -79bp and +8.5% YTD, SocGen Trend -75bp and +8.3% YTD, while the short-term traders index lagged at -1.71% in July and +3.34% YTD.
insights.speaker: Niels (host)
insights.so_what: Trend programs kept most of a strong first-half gain through a choppy July, so drawdown-driven redemption pressure on managed futures looks limited going into August.

insights.claim: Traditional beta was negative in July 2026 with S&P 500 total return -2.39% (though +7.58% YTD), MSCI World -1.63%, MSCI World ex-US-and-Canada only -26bp and +9.56% YTD, and the S&P US Aggregate Bond index -91bp and flat for the year.
insights.speaker: Niels (host)
insights.so_what: Bonds again offered no offset to an equity drawdown, and non-US equity leadership year-to-date argues against home-country concentration.

insights.claim: A Hong Kong-listed 2x levered ETF on Korean chipmaker SK Hynix is down 47% over three months while SK Hynix itself is up 1%, after the underlying was up as much as 125% and the ETF as much as 300% inside that window — a clean demonstration of volatility drag from daily-reset leverage.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: Daily-reset leverage turns a round trip in the underlying into permanent capital loss, making levered ETF holders structural forced sellers and the products a wealth transfer rather than exposure.
insights.quote: these two times levered ETFs in Hong Kong on the listed chip makers in Korea

insights.claim: Over a long enough horizon every levered ETF mathematically approaches zero, because geometric returns are penalized by variance so the drawdown effect dominates the draw-up effect through time.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: Treat levered ETFs as decaying short-vol-like instruments to trade tactically or short structurally, never to hold strategically.
insights.quote: over a long enough time horizon all levered ETFs approach zero

themes.theme: Markets as complex adaptive systems, not distributions

insights.claim: Dredge frames markets as Lorenz-style dynamics — infinite paths inside a finite space chasing an unattainable strange attractor — so the job is to understand current initial conditions and be resilient to an unknowable path rather than forecast the path.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: Shifts portfolio effort from forecast accuracy to survivability under paths that were never in the sample.
insights.quote: infinite paths inside a finite space chasing an unattainable strange attractor

insights.claim: The future is not hidden information waiting to be uncovered — it has not been written yet — because knowing what happens in five days would require knowing the decisions and conglomerated positions of every agent transacting until then, making the system computationally irreducible.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: If outcomes are irreducible rather than merely uncertain, spending on better forecasts has a hard ceiling while spending on response capability does not.
insights.quote: the future isn't hidden. It hasn't been written yet.

insights.claim: Mandelbrot showed in 1960 that markets have roughness at every scale like the coastline of England, so a single fixed ruler gives different answers at each scale and only the scaling dimension is meaningful — a finding finance has resisted for six decades while staying in a Euclidean, linear world.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Risk measured at one horizon cannot be rescaled to another with square-root-of-time, which invalidates most standard risk aggregation.
insights.quote: it's it's a maths that's it's a correct form of maths but it's not a maths to apply to this domain

insights.claim: Markets differ from physical systems like weather because their agents are reflexive — they adapt to the system while the system forces adaptation on them — which Brennan illustrates with Feynman's line about how hard physics would be if electrons had feelings.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Models validated on physical-system data or stationary backtests systematically understate other participants' adaptation to your own trades.
insights.quote: imagine how hard physics would be if electrons have feelings

themes.theme: Price-insensitive flow and the unresolved bond imbalance

insights.claim: Dredge models participants as 'rational accounting man' — price-insensitive actors following accounting rules, regulation and annual compensation cycles — versus 'boundedly rational agents' with skin in the game, and argues the former dominates most markets because bank, pension, insurance, central bank and FX-reserve traders all belong to it.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: Most marginal flow is not valuation-driven, so positioning and rule-driven constraints predict price better than fundamentals.
insights.quote: one of my famous dredgisms is positioning is the only thing that matters

insights.claim: Dredge tells Mike Green and Harry Krishnan their passive-equity work misses the bigger elephant: the bond market blew through any reasonable price-insensitive-ownership threshold at the peak of what he calls the mother of all bond bubbles in late 2020.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: The passive-distortion thesis applies with more force to fixed income than equities, making rates the likeliest venue for the next liquidity accident.
insights.quote: you're missing the biggest elephant in the room, which is the bond market

insights.claim: The 2022 rate shock was only the initial unwind of the bond imbalance and the complexity remains unresolved, because central banks, FX reserve managers, banks, pension funds and insurers still hold massive unrealized losses with no positions cut, no capital freed and no accounting losses recognized.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: A large latent supply of forced selling and capital impairment remains, arguing for owning convexity to further rate dislocations instead of assuming the shock is over.
insights.quote: Nobody's freed the capital that's tied up in those things or the lack of capital. Nobody's recognized the accounting losses.

insights.claim: Pension funds and insurers have masked duration inside duration-extending callable note structures with embedded Bermudan swaptions, and those structured products now carry very large unrealized losses that have not been recognized.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: Hidden short optionality in the institutional hunt for structured yield is both the supply Dredge buys against and the source of future forced hedging flows.

insights.claim: What moves prices is accumulating imbalance: price-insensitive flow builds reflexively as leverage is applied under a regulatory construct in which volatility is the measure of risk and leverage on a low-volatility tranche supposedly adds none, then reverses in a fat tail once the mistake is recognized.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: Fat tails are largely a policy artifact, so the trade is to own the tail wherever regulation has certified something as low risk.
insights.quote: the leverage is the risk. It's the reason why it's a left skewed return distribution

themes.theme: Endogenous risk: the 25% divergent threshold and the danger of calm

insights.claim: Once roughly 25% or more of participants in Brennan's model are divergent (trend-amplifying), every real-market signature — fat tails, volatility clustering and market memory — appears at once as a phase transition rather than gradually.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: A measurable share of amplifying flow is the switch between benign and tail-prone regimes, reframing fat tails as a structural feature rather than an anomaly.
insights.quote: As soon as I start putting those divergent population in there of 25% and above, boom, all the signatures come back into the market.

insights.claim: Passive investing is a divergent, amplifying participant in Brennan's taxonomy: it is price-insensitive but its rule — invest in the biggest things — applies a directional amplifying force to price.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Rising passive share pushes markets toward and past the divergent threshold, implying secularly fatter tails and more clustered volatility.
insights.quote: It's not that they are responding to price. They are price insensitive. They're responding to a rule but that rule is invest in the biggest things.

insights.claim: Cited microstructure research found roughly 90% of market moves come from endogenous sources rather than news, with no strong tick-by-tick correlation between news events and price moves, and Brennan's own models reproduced all real-market signatures with no news events at all.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Risk budgets organized around scheduled events are mis-specified; market state and positioning are the variables to monitor.
insights.quote: it was 90% of the moves were from indogenous sources

insights.claim: Large moves build progressively rather than arriving from nowhere: activity picks up beforehand, liquidity quietly thins, the order book turns fragile, a trigger fires, and it takes longer to settle afterwards because markets are inelastic and carry memory.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Thinning depth plus rising activity in a quiet tape are observable pre-conditions for a tail event and can be monitored directly.
insights.quote: liquidity quietly thins out. The book therefore gets very fragile and then bang it goes with a trigger

insights.claim: Dredge's forest-fire framework comes from self-organized criticality (Per Bak's How Nature Works): fire risk grows the longer a forest goes unburned because clogged brush accumulates, diversification only protects against a lightning strike on one tree, and in markets the brush that carries fire between trees is leverage while correlation is what makes diversification fail.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: Monitor connectivity — leverage and correlation — rather than the number of holdings, because connectivity converts a local loss into a portfolio loss.
insights.quote: In the financial markets, that would be leverage.

insights.claim: Because Value at Risk measures only the short-term frequency of past fires, it reports no risk exactly where fragility is highest, which is also where insurance is cheapest — Dredge says he does not need to know which trees a client owns, only where the driest brush is.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: This is the core hedge-selection rule: screen for assets whose realized volatility and VaR are lowest relative to structural fragility, then buy convexity there.
insights.quote: I don't need to know. I just need to know where the most dry brush is.

insights.claim: Volatility-targeted position sizing mechanically increases size during calm periods while managers simultaneously lever up behaviourally to earn a living in a low-return tape, so leverage is fed into the system precisely when the next shock will do most damage.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Volatility targeting is a pro-cyclical leverage machine, so a hard cap on notional leverage is the fix.
insights.quote: their models mechanistically increase the position size in that period of calm because they're saying it's a safe market

insights.claim: Brennan's modelling finds most risk events originate in calm regimes hit by a volatility shock rather than in already-volatile regimes, citing a Japanese bond market episode around 2018 where roughly 9% trailing volatility authorized about 16.4x leverage so that a roughly 6% move destroyed about 9% of capital.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Stress tests should be run from the lowest-volatility states, because that is where authorized leverage and realized loss potential peak.
insights.quote: do not acqu you know equate calmness with safety

themes.theme: Path dependence: ergodicity, Kelly and Sharpe's blindness

insights.claim: In an ergodic process the ensemble average equals the time average (arithmetic mean equals geometric mean); investing is non-ergodic, so the path decides the outcome — a 50% drawdown needs a 100% recovery, and in a multi-lap race a crash means you do not finish.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: Any metric that averages across scenarios rather than compounding through time systematically overstates achievable wealth.
insights.quote: a 50% draw down isn't corrected with a 50% recovery. You're not back. You got to get a 100% recovery to get back.

insights.claim: Reshuffling 40 years of returns leaves Sharpe, Sortino, variance, VaR and standard deviation unchanged while terminal wealth falls by between 30% and 84% depending on the ordering.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Two managers with identical risk statistics can differ enormously in realized wealth, so diligence must examine sequencing and construction, not ratios.
insights.quote: this isn't a spread we're talking about. This is the difference between a bad year and not being in business.

insights.claim: Being optimal forgoes the room to be wrong: the Kelly criterion asks what fraction of capital maximizes growth given a known edge, placing you on a peak where any overshoot moves you quickly toward risk of ruin while under-betting buys error tolerance cheaply.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Deliberately under-betting relative to an optimum is the practical way to price in estimation error and non-stationarity.
insights.quote: the problem of being optimal is that it foregoes the room for being wrong

insights.claim: Kelly sizing rests on an estimate rather than reality, and including fat tails explodes the sample size needed for a reliable estimate, so no market ever supplies enough data to justify betting at the optimum in a non-stationary system.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Estimation error, not the formula, binds optimal sizing, which permanently caps prudent leverage below the theoretical optimum.
insights.quote: To be optimal, you've got to have perfect information. And we never have that perfect information in these complex adaptive systems.

insights.claim: Brennan tested Kelly-based sizing against simple equal-risk fractional sizing on his trend-following systems and the simple rule outperformed once regime changes and realistic noise were introduced, because the noise is often larger than the signal used to compute the optimal bet — with Long-Term Capital Management the canonical case of optimality working until the assumptions broke.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Equal-risk sizing is not a naive compromise but the empirically better choice under non-stationarity, and is directly implementable.

insights.claim: October 2008 was the single best month in Brennan's 40-year trend-following history and contributed 3.4% of total portfolio wealth, yet the Sharpe ratio moved only from 0.914 to 0.931 — about two cents in the dollar of credit for the payoff that mattered most.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Sharpe structurally penalizes convex return streams, so allocators screening on Sharpe systematically reject the strategies that pay in crises.
insights.quote: So it paid 2 cents in the dollar Neil. So the sharp penalizes trend followers.

insights.claim: Two portfolios can both show a Sharpe of 1.5 while one is a single Kelly-levered concentrated bet resting on one estimate and the other is a wide book of loosely related small positions, because Sharpe compresses everything into an average and a volatility and discards how the portfolio was assembled — one rope across a canyon versus a thousand strands.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Manager selection should interrogate failure modes and architecture, since the headline ratio cannot distinguish one strand from a thousand.
insights.quote: the number records where you arrive but it doesn't record how you got there

themes.theme: Diversification, permanent coupling and fractal tails

insights.claim: Diversification protects sometimes but not when it matters most, because it assumes stable correlation and ignores connectivity between holdings; Dredge's earlier paper argued that diversifying across many positions any one of which can cost all your capital is not diversification at all.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: Screen holdings for unbounded downside before counting them as diversifiers, because a single unbounded exposure makes breadth irrelevant.
insights.quote: Yes, sometimes right just not when it matters the most right.

insights.claim: A thousand strands across a canyon all attached to one anchor at each end still has a single failure mode while looking diversified — the analogue of borrowing short and lending long across a dozen markets, which is really one interest-rate bet.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Map shared anchors — funding, duration, a single policy variable — across strategies, because correlation statistics will not reveal them in calm periods.
insights.quote: imagine if they're all connected to a single anchor at each end of that canyon. There is still one failure mode there, but it looks diversified.

insights.claim: Brennan argues markets are permanently coupled rather than becoming correlated only in crises, because individual agents hold diversified books across products and that shared behaviour creates continuous coupling; what changes in a crisis is the phase, from cancelling oscillation to aligned trend.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Correlation is a phase reading of always-on coupling, so measured low correlation in calm markets must never be used to size crisis risk.
insights.quote: I think that markets are always permanently coupled

insights.claim: Brennan's research finds diversification does not thin the tails: kurtosis initially drops as positions are added and then ramps back up, because in a fractal market a larger sample exposes you to larger structures — sampling a tree gives leaves at small scale and trunks at large scale.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Wide books should expect both their largest drawdown and largest gain to grow with breadth, so drawdown expectations must scale up rather than down with diversification.
insights.quote: in my research I found that diversification doesn't thin the tails

insights.claim: Maximal diversification is valued for right-tail access rather than volatility reduction: Brennan's book held cocoa when it exploded precisely because a small portfolio of majors — currencies and bonds — would never have carried the position.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Market-count breadth is the mechanism for capturing idiosyncratic explosions, favouring the widest-universe trend managers over the most efficient-looking ones.
insights.quote: We had that idiosyncratic exposure to cocoa because we are maximally diversified.

insights.claim: Across 125 years of Dow Jones plus S&P 500 data the major material moves are where all the information is and the rest is noise, and because fractals are scale-invariant your largest drawdown and largest return are always still ahead of you as the sample grows.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Never treat the historical maximum drawdown as a bound; size so that a larger-than-observed move remains survivable.
insights.quote: your draw down is always bigger ahead of you as will the greater returns will always be ahead of you as you increase your sample size

themes.theme: Architecting convexity: bought optionality versus trend

insights.claim: Dredge overlays a Gaussian curve on a football pitch to show it measures only frequency — where the ball spends time — then overlays a Shannon entropy curve of information value, showing the 10 worst and 10 best months out of 480 contribute almost all of the S&P's long-term compounded return.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: If about 2% of months drive nearly all compounding, portfolio design should optimize behaviour in those months rather than average-period efficiency.
insights.quote: The average is meaningless. It is a wasted statistic.

insights.claim: Dredge and colleague Nick built a FIFA-data model of the World Cup producing a 'convex goalkeeper theorem' with three layers — defensive resilience approaching your own penalty box (most important), attacking efficiency approaching the opponent's box (second), and individual tail performance such as last-minute goals (third) — because a knockout tournament is non-ergodic: hit the ruin barrier and you are out.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: An empirical demonstration that defence dominates offence in survival games, supporting a hedging-first ordering of portfolio spend.
insights.quote: we came up with what's we've called the convex goalkeeper theorem

insights.claim: When England went one up against Argentina and parked the bus they did what the investment industry does constantly — tried to reduce risk by capping upside, the equivalent of selling call options or shifting into 60/40 — retaining full downside while giving up the attacking that constitutes good defence.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: Covered-call and bond-ballast de-risking is a concave trade that removes upside without removing tail risk, a direct argument against yield-enhancement overlays.
insights.quote: They thought they could reduce risk by capping the upside.

insights.claim: Dredge describes a double-to-triple whammy of mispricing: buying long-dated implicit leverage priced off a flawed distribution of the underlying, where volatility supply is dominated by price-insensitive structured-product sellers whose product is itself mispriced relative to its own distribution and carries added nonlinearity in its construction.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: The identified edge is layered mispricing in long-dated volatility created by regulated sellers, which is where a long-vol allocation should be pointed.

insights.claim: Dredge advises owning assets with thin tails and high natural volatility where upside compensates for downside risk, and constructing hedges from things with fat left tails and artificially suppressed volatility that attract explicit repo and banking leverage or implicit leverage via volatility selling.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: A directly implementable screen: hold high-natural-volatility thin-tail assets, hedge with low-volatility fat-left-tail leveraged assets.
insights.quote: you want to own and invest in things with thin tails, things that have high natural volatility

insights.claim: A long position with a stop is a synthetic call and a short with a stop is a synthetic put, so trend followers do pay an option premium — in whipsaw losses, foregone growth and psychological cost — even though it never appears as a line item the way Dredge's option premium does.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Comparing trend to long-vol on visible cost is misleading; both pay a premium, only the accounting location differs.
insights.quote: That's a synthetic call. A short position with a stop is is a synthetic put.

insights.claim: Dredge's approach is constrained by the need for efficient volatility markets and volatility supply, which is why Convex Strategies had no cocoa position while trend followers did — nobody brought them a volatility structure in it, and trend's breadth of markets cannot be matched with options.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: The two convexity sources cover different parts of the distribution and different market sets, a concrete case for combining them in one allocation.
insights.quote: Every way you can add convexity add convexity. That's the answer to everyone's problem.

insights.claim: Adding 50% long-vol to 50% S&P — and equally 50% trend to 50% S&P on capital — produces something close to the sum of the two return streams rather than their average, per a chart in Dredge's June paper that the host says he replicates for trend following.
insights.speaker: Niels (host)
insights.so_what: This combination effect is the empirical case for return stacking and portable-alpha structures built on convex sleeves.
insights.quote: you don't just get an average, you kind of almost get the sum

insights.claim: Dredge resolves the portable-alpha leverage objection with concavity versus convexity: most investors lever concave risks whose correlation is low in good markets and rises in bad ones, adding volatility drag and creating disasters, whereas levering explicitly negatively correlating convex risk is risk-reducing as the position grows, so hedge and risk can be added iteratively.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: Judge leverage by the convexity of what is levered rather than by notional — a usable test for evaluating return-stacked products.
insights.quote: most people are levering concave risks

insights.claim: When positively convex, more risk is less risk — a principle Dredge dates to running Bankers Trust businesses through the Asian crisis — because non-recourse leverage bought via options means the more hedge you add, the more risk you can afford to take.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: This is the mechanism by which a hedging budget raises rather than lowers portfolio expected growth, limited only by hedge availability and price.
insights.quote: when you're positively convex, more risk is less risk

themes.theme: What allocators should change Monday morning

insights.claim: Dredge says the first thing that must change is the fiduciary incentive structure, because everyone is paid on calendar-year arithmetic returns that ignore the non-ergodic compounding path, and expected return is a nonsensical number that has destroyed more wealth for capital owners than almost anything while arguably transferring it to fiduciaries.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: Annual-return incentives are the root cause of concave institutional portfolios, so mandate terms and fee clocks are the highest-leverage thing an asset owner can change.
insights.quote: Expected return is a nonsensical number and it's destroyed more wealth for capital owners than maybe any other simple thing.

insights.claim: Because you cannot optimize to an unknown future path, Dredge's prescription is to install brakes first and then learn by doing — trial and error on aerodynamics, engine, tyres — building resilience to divergence from expectation instead of optimizing to a backward-looking expectation, and freeing capital from ballast held only to slow the portfolio down.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: Replaces backtest-optimized allocation with an iterative brakes-first process: shrink low-return ballast, buy explicit convexity, redeploy released capital into upside participation.
insights.quote: you can't optimize to the unknown future path. All you can do is put brakes on your car and go out and learn how to drive.

insights.claim: Brennan's first concrete rule is to cap leverage in absolute terms — with no statistical justification other than breaking the automatic link between a quiet market and a large position — because most capital destruction comes from quiet markets carrying too much size, and leverage is a destruction of compounding.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: A hard notional cap overrides volatility targeting's pro-cyclicality and is implementable immediately in any systematic program.
insights.quote: cap leverage and absolute terms

insights.claim: Brennan's second rule is to size every market to the same risk rather than tilting toward whichever edge currently looks strongest, because differences between edges are smaller than the noise in measuring them, making a ranking a signal too faint to trust and a tilt a quiet rebuild of the single-cable failure mode.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Equal-risk sizing across markets is what preserves access to unexpected winners like cocoa; strength-ranked tilts systematically exclude them.
insights.quote: So a ranking is a signal too faint to trust

insights.claim: Brennan's third rule is to grow returns by widening the book — adding different systems and more diversification — rather than scaling bets on existing holdings, which is the difference between a heavier load on one cable and more cables on the bridge.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Meet return targets with breadth rather than leverage, which also increases fractal right-tail exposure.
insights.quote: grow by widening the book, not by scaling the bets

insights.claim: Brennan's fourth rule is to enter small and let the market build the position out of open profit rather than using size, positioning or leverage to impose a view on the market.
insights.speaker: Richard Brennan
insights.so_what: Scaling on unrealized gains rather than at entry keeps risk of ruin low while retaining right-tail participation.
insights.quote: always enter small and let the market build the position out of open profit

insights.claim: Dredge's closing position is that there is no magic model, formula or regulatory rule for risk — risk is about accountability, tacit knowledge and recognizing that if you crash you are out of the race — and until that is instilled in price-insensitive rational accounting men the system stays permanently fragile.
insights.speaker: Dave Dredge
insights.so_what: Structural fragility is a permanent feature of the regulated system, which sustains the long-run opportunity in owning cheap convexity.
insights.quote: risk is about accountability
